source_text: Nec hoc solum, fratres dilectissimi, animaduertere et intellegere debemus, quod appellemus patrem qui sit in caelis, sed coniungimus et dicimus pater noster, idest eorum qui credunt, eorum qui per eum sanctificati et gratiae spiritalis natiuitate reparati filii Dei esse coeperunt. quae uox Iudaeos etiam perstringit et percutit, quia Christum sibi per prophetas adnuntiatum et ad se prius missum non tantum spreuerunt infideliter sed et crudeliter necauerunt: qui iam non possunt patrem Dominum uocare, cum Dominus eos confundat et redarguat dicens: uos de diabolo patre nati estis et concupiscentias patris uestri facere uultis. ille enim homicida fuit ab initio et in ueritate non stetit, quia ueritas non est in illo. et per Esaiam prophetam Deus clamat indignans: filios generaui et exaltaui, ipsi autem me spreuerunt. agnouit bos possessorem suum et asinus praesepium domini sui: Israel autem me non cognouit et populus me non intellexit. uae genti peccatrici, populo pleno peccatis, semen nequam, filii scelesti. dereliquistis Dominum et in indignationem misistis illum sanctum Israel. in quorum exprobrationem christiani quando oramus pater noster dicimus, quia noster esse iam coepit et Iudaeorum qui eum dereliquerunt esse desiuit. nec peccator populus potest esse filius, sed quibus remissa peccatorum datur, eis filiorum nomen adscribitur, eis et aeternitas repromittitur Domino ipso dicente: omnis qui facit peccatum seruus est. seruus autem non manet in domo in aeternum, filius manet in aeternum.
thought_title: Only the reborn may call God Father
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the opening words of the Lord's Prayer, now focusing on the word 'our' and its exclusion of the Jews who rejected Christ.
pass_a_gloss: Nor this only, most beloved brothers, we ought to notice and understand, that we call Father him who is in heaven, but we join and say our Father, that is of those who believe, of those who through him sanctified and by the spiritual birth of grace restored have begun to be children of God. This word also strikes and smites the Jews, because Christ announced to them through the prophets and sent to them first they not only rejected faithlessly but also killed cruelly: who now cannot call the Lord Father, since the Lord confounds and rebukes them saying: you were born of the devil father and the desires of your father you wish to do. For he was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. And through Isaiah the prophet God cries out indignant: I have begotten sons and exalted them, but they have rejected me. The ox knew its owner and the donkey the manger of its lord: but Israel did not know me and my people did not understand me. Woe to the sinful nation, to the people full of sins, wicked seed, criminal children. You have forsaken the Lord and have provoked to indignation the Holy One of Israel. In reproach of whom Christians when we pray say our Father, because he has already begun to be ours and has ceased to be of the Jews who forsook him. Nor can a sinful people be a son, but to those to whom forgiveness of sins is given, to them the name of children is ascribed, to them also eternity is promised, the Lord himself saying: everyone who commits sin is a slave. But the slave does not remain in the house forever, the son remains forever.

choices.english: restored by the spiritual birth of grace
choices.why: Keeps the passive participle 'reparati' as 'restored' and preserves the instrumental ablative 'natiuitate' as 'by the birth', matching the literal force of the clause.
'uox' here refers to the utterance 'our Father'; 'this word' keeps the demonstrative force and avoids the misleading 'voice'.
The two verbs are distinct: 'perstringit' is a grazing or glancing blow, 'percutit' a full blow; rendering both as 'strikes and smites' preserves the intensification.
Keeps the noun 'seed' literally rather than 'offspring', and 'criminal children' preserves the strong negative force of 'scelesti'.
The Latin phrase 'in indignationem mittere' means to provoke to anger; the rendering keeps the noun 'indignation' and the verb 'provoked'.

choices.term: omnis qui facit peccatum seruus est
choices.english: everyone who commits sin is a slave
choices.why: Keeps 'facit peccatum' as 'commits sin' and 'seruus' as 'slave', matching the literal wording of the citation.

pass_b_english: Nor should we only notice and understand this, dearly beloved brothers, that we call upon the Father who is in heaven. We also join ourselves together and say “our Father”—that is, the Father of those who believe, of those who have been sanctified through him and restored by the spiritual birth of grace, and so have begun to be children of God. This word also strikes and smites the Jews, because they not only faithlessly rejected Christ, who had been announced to them through the prophets and sent to them first, but cruelly killed him. They can no longer call the Lord “Father,” since the Lord confounds and rebukes them, saying: “You were born of your father the devil, and you want to carry out your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him” (John 8:44). And through the prophet Isaiah God cries out in indignation: “I have begotten children and raised them up, but they have rejected me. The ox knows its owner and the donkey its master’s manger, but Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood. Woe to a sinful nation, a people full of sins, wicked seed, criminal children. You have forsaken the Lord and have provoked to indignation the Holy One of Israel” (Isaiah 1:2-4). To their reproach, when we Christians pray we say “our Father,” because he has now begun to be ours and has ceased to be the Father of the Jews who abandoned him. Nor can a sinful people be children; rather, to those to whom forgiveness of sins is given, the name of children is assigned, and to them eternity is promised, as the Lord himself says: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave. A slave does not remain in the house forever; a son remains forever” (John 8:34-35).

last_rejected.quote: We also join ourselves together and say “our Father”
last_rejected.source_quote: sed coniungimus et dicimus pater noster
last_rejected.why: coniungimus adds the word “our” to “Father”; it does not mean the speakers join themselves together.
last_rejected.fix: But we add to it and say “our Father”—that is, the Father of those who believe.
last_rejected.ruling: Cyprian's "coniungimus et dicimus pater noster" means we join (the word 'our') / unite ourselves in saying; 'join ourselves together' is within range and conveys the communal sense.
